items.title: David N. Baker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] I think it’s Free Play, isn’t it? >> [INTERVIEWEE] Free Play [by Stephen Nachmanovitch].

ctx.x: I think it’s Free Play, isn’t it?

Free Play [by Stephen Nachmanovitch]. Yeah. I'm sorry about that. [laughter] Yeah. Free Play. And there are any number of other books. But I’m not sure that most people understand how the muse works. I’ve talked to a lot of people who tell me

different ways to call the muse. I write so much music that usually I don’t have a chance to sit around and wait for inspiration. I have to write because I’m being paid to write. So I’ve devised a number of schemes. Some of them come from other teachers. I’ve had a teacher tell me – when I wrote the piece Kosbro, he said, “Why don’t you go sit in the auditorium where the piece will probably be played and imagine what you’re going to hear.” And I did. And I sat down and I wrote the piece. I have no notion of where…
